title: Find every cut vertex in one pass
description:
A vertex of an undirected graph is a cut vertex when deleting it, together with every edge that touches it, leaves the graph in more separate pieces than it was in before.

Implement a function called ArticulationPoints that receives the number of vertices and an adjacency list, and returns every cut vertex of that graph in ascending order. Vertices are numbered from zero. The adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the vertices it shares an edge with; every edge appears in both directions.

ArticulationPoints(5, [[1, 2, 3], [0, 2], [0, 1], [0, 4], [3]]) -> [0, 3]. That graph is a triangle on 0, 1, 2 with a tail 0 - 3 - 4: deleting 0 strands the pair 1, 2 from the pair 3, 4, and deleting 3 strands 4 on its own, while deleting any other vertex leaves one connected piece.

A graph with no cut vertex returns an empty list. A four-vertex ring is the smallest example: ArticulationPoints(4, [[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 3], [0, 2]]) -> [].

The hidden tests hold you to three more things. The graph is not guaranteed to be connected, so every piece of it has to be examined, not just the piece the first vertex is in. A vertex with no edges at all is never a cut vertex, because deleting it leaves the rest of the graph exactly as it was. And the returned list is always sorted ascending, whatever order you happen to discover the vertices in.

This card asks for the optimal solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of over a hundred thousand vertices with a two second budget. Deleting one vertex at a time and recounting the pieces gives the right answer but is far too slow to pass. The whole graph has to be settled in a single traversal that visits each vertex and each edge once, in time proportional to their total.
objective: Recall and implement the linear-time, single-traversal algorithm for finding the cut vertices of an undirected graph.
